title: Opinion Formation in a Spatially Constrained Coevolving Nonlinear Voter Model
authors: Phil Gwon Kim, Jaeyong Bae, Jaeseok Hur, Hawoong Jeong
abstract: We investigate a spatially constrained coevolving nonlinear voter model. Using a random geometric graph, we constrain the interaction range of voter dynamics. If local rewiring is not possible, the discordant link is deleted. Our results reveal absorbing states that differ not only in magnetization and activity, but also in mean degree and spatial state organization. By exploring dynamical and structural observables, we found that distinct regimes from the existing coevolving nonlinear voter model are characterized by a reduced consensus region, spatially segregated fragmentation, and isolated node formation. Additionally, we develop a phenomenological description of the evolution of the mean degree and terminal non-conserved quantities that is consistent with the numerical results. Our model highlights how local geometric accessibility reshapes the structure of the absorbing states.
summary: This paper analyzes a nonlinear voter model where social interactions occur on a spatially constrained network. By incorporating rules that delete links when rewiring fails, the authors show that global consensus is fragile. Instead, the system settles into fragmented absorbing states whose structure depends critically on the interplay between local geometry and interaction parameters.
main_problem: The study investigates opinion formation dynamics in a spatially constrained coevolving nonlinear voter model, focusing on how local geometric constraints alter the nature of absorbing states.
main_result: Local geometric accessibility fundamentally reshapes the structure of absorbing states, leading to distinct regimes characterized by reduced consensus regions and spatially segregated fragmentation rather than robust global consensus.
method: The authors employ extensive numerical simulations across parameter space $(p, q)$ on a Random Geometric Graph (RGG), utilizing techniques like finite-size scaling and route closure equations to characterize absorption processes.
model_or_system: The model is a Nonlinear Voter Model implemented on an RGG embedded in 2D space. Dynamics involve state flips and rewiring attempts, with the crucial modification being link deletion when local rewiring fails due to spatial constraints.
key_observables: Magnetization ($\langle|m|angle$), active link density ($\langlehoangle$), largest connected component fraction ($\langle S_{max}/Nangle$), mean degree ($\langle kangle$), and the spatial enrichment ($\Delta sp$).
important_parameters: The interaction probability ($p$) and the rewiring/coevolution parameter ($q$); system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that deviations from standard CNVM due to link deletion are key; finite-size effects are noted when interpreting consensus regimes.
figures_summary: Figures map out empirical regimes (P1-P5) based on multiple observables, showing size dependence of magnetization loss (Fig. 2), and distinguishing between topological vs. real-space fragmentation using spatial enrichment ($\Delta sp$) (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the model by first defining the constrained dynamics, then mapping out empirical regimes via multiple observables, developing phenomenological descriptions for mean degree evolution, and finally applying advanced techniques like finite-time scaling to characterize absorption boundaries.
why_interesting: While focused on classical opinion dynamics, the framework of non-equilibrium phase transitions, absorbing states, and structural changes due to local constraints (like link deletion) mirrors concepts in quantum many-body systems undergoing localization or fragmentation.

(b,c) Represen- tative absorbing configurations for P3 and P2, respectively. P3 illustrates spatially segregated fragmentation, whereas P2 illustrates mainly topological fragmentation with weak real- space segregation.

Fig. 3(a) shows that P3 is distinguished from the other absorbing fragmented regimes by a strong enhancement of the spatial enrichment. For instance, P2 can be both absorbing and fragmented in the graph-theoretic sense, but it exhibits only weak spatial enrichment. Thus, P2 primarily represents topological fragmentation, in which discordant links are removed without significant real- space separation of the two state types. In contrast, P3 corresponds to spatially segregated fragmentation, in which graph fragmentation is accompanied by real-space state-domain separation.
